4726.prule: Stress is predictable and falls on the last syllable of the root, irrespective of suffixes; prefixes/proclitics and suffixes (modifiers, directionals, negator -tap, object markers) are unstressed. Word-final only when the root is word-final.

4730.dq: The Pearic word seems to have the same canonic shape as the word in most other Mon-Khmer languages. It consists of a single stressed syllable which may be preceded by a weakly stressed pre-syllable.
4730.dloc: Sec. 2.1 'Contemporary phonetic system', p. 429 (last paragraph) continuing on p. 431 (first sentence); pp. 2 and 4.
4730.prule: Word = one stressed main syllable, optionally preceded by one weakly stressed presyllable whose nucleus is a neutral vowel /ə/: stress falls on the final (main) syllable of the sesquisyllabic word, whatever the main syllable's shape C1(C2)V1(F1). Positional and quantity-insensitive as stated (no condition on the main syllable's vowel length or coda). Stated for the Pearic branch as a whole ('the Pearic word'), over a ten-dialect sample that explicitly includes Somray of Battambang (Martin's SY and Baradat's WP, both Kranhung) and Samre of Siem Reap; grids for the only word shapes the source covers: 1 and 01.
4730.srule: None: 'It consists of a single stressed syllable which may be preceded by a weakly stressed pre-syllable' (the presyllable has a neutral vowel /ə/; words are at most presyllable + main syllable; no secondary or rhythmic stress described).

tn.quote: Le lohëhendo possède deux unités tonales de base: 1. Le ton bas, noté [x ou B] 2. Le ton haut, noté ['ou H] ... Ces deux tons peuvent se combiner et être portés par une même unité porteuse à l'intérieur d'un mot; c'est la contonalité qui produit des tons composés. Sous cette forme composée, le ton revêt quatre configurations reparties en deux groupes: Les tons modulés et les tons ondulés. Les premiers comprennent: 1. Le ton descendant, noté [Λ ou HB] 2. Le ton montant, noté [" ou BH]
tn.translation: Lohëhendo has two basic tonal units: 1. the low tone, written [` or B (=L)]; 2. the high tone, written [´ or H] ... These two tones can combine and be carried by one and the same bearing unit inside a word; this 'contonality' produces compound tones. In compound form the tone takes four configurations in two groups: modulated tones and undulating tones. The former comprise: 1. the falling tone, written [^ or HL]; 2. the rising tone, written [ˇ or LH]
tn.cite: Ngonga-ke-Mbembe, E. Hubert O. 2009. Langage initiatique ohendo: phonologie et métaphonologie des langues dérivées. PhD dissertation, Radboud Universiteit Nijmegen. Chapter V (phonology of lohëhendo), sections 5.2.3 'Les tons', 5.8.3 'L'accent', 5.8.4 'Les tons'.

4735.heavy: Not defined in the relayed passage. The rule is stated as mora-counting ('stress assignment is mora-sensitive'; 'stress is assigned on the penultimate voiced mora'), with 'voiceless moras being treated as extrametrical'. Which syllables are bimoraic (long vowels, diphthongs, codas or geminates) is not said.
4735.dflt: Not stated. If every syllable is a single voiced mora the penultimate mora is the penultimate syllable; if the final vowel is devoiced (extrametrical) the penultimate voiced mora is the antepenultimate syllable, while high pitch stays on the penultimate syllable.
4735.prule: Hypothesis (Rehg 1993: 32, relayed by Vita 2020: 19): primary stress on the penultimate voiced mora, counting from the right edge; voiceless (devoiced word-final) moras are extrametrical and do not count, so a word with a devoiced final vowel is stressed one mora further left than the surface penult. High pitch (level 3 of the 231 contour) sits on the penultimate syllable, so stress and pitch peak can fall apart when the final vowel is devoiced.
4735.srule: Not mentioned in Vita 2020: 19 + fn. 1 (relay of Rehg 1993: 32), the only stress passage about Pulo Annian/Sonsorol; section 4 'Micronesian Prosody' pp. 17-19 read. 4736.dq: It seems to me, however, that stress-accent is important in So, not on the paradigmatic level, but rather on the syntagmatic level. ... Within the domain of a bisyllabic word stem, stress falls on the first syllable ... It is surely no coincidence that the intonation contour rises clause-finally and that most accented syllables are found in an immediate pre-pausal position
4736.prule: Stress is non-distinctive (not lexical, no tone) and its position is set by morphological make-up: in a bare bisyllabic word stem stress falls on the first syllable ('lakʷan 'child'); when a derivational suffix is added it 'generally' falls on the final syllable, i.e. on the suffix (lakʷa'n-a 'my child', ko-ken-'k-as 'I will be killed', ʊrʊ'm-ac 'gather up'). Carlin frames this as a syntagmatic organizational feature: accented syllables cluster in immediate pre-pausal position and mark prominent clause elements.

4738.dq: Ударение в именных частях речи и в наречиях падает на последний слог слова: estā̊ré ‘звезда’, rušán ‘светлый’, digé ‘другой’, pånjá ‘пятьдесят’, hâmišé ‘всегда’. (p. 154; 'the last syllable of the word', stated for parts of speech, with a separate word-level rule for verb forms; Christensen § 38 separately lists the unaccented clitics of the phrase.)
4738.dloc: Rastorgueva 1999: p. 154 (Sorkhei article, section 'Foneticheskie svedenija', 3rd paragraph); pp. 149-150 (belt article). Christensen 1935: p. 35 § 38.
4738.prule: Word stress on the final syllable of the word in nouns, adjectives, pronouns, numerals and adverbs (Sorkhei p. 154 categorical: 'падает на последний слог слова'; Aftari p. 165 'обычно' = usually; belt article pp. 149-150 the same rule for Sorkhei, Lasgerdi, Biyabanaki, Aftari). Syllable weight is never mentioned; the pattern is the Persian type (Christensen § 35: 'les mêmes règles que le persan'). The ezafe -e and the indefinite/unit marker -i are unstressed, so stress stays on the last stem syllable.
4738.srule: Stated only for verb forms, placed by morphology: when the main stress falls on a verbal prefix (derivational ha-, da-, du-, va-; be-/me-; negation nå-/ne-), the personal ending carries a secondary stress ('основное ударение падает на префикс, вспомогательное — на окончание': hákennìm 'we make', hákårdàm 'I made', dábåstàm, dúrizìn, váporsìn, vanǻporsìn; p. 150 vǻporsìn, békatìm, mébordàm). Christensen 1935 § 37 (first-hand): with a prefix the ending 'porte ordinairement en sourkhéī... un accent secondaire, qui peut paraître parfois presque aussi fort que l'accent du préfixe'; § 36 the preterite ending may carry a secondary accent. No secondary stress is mentioned for nouns, adjectives, pronouns, numerals or adverbs (final main stress only).

4739.dq: 'Drawling' in general is due to the absence of stress accent, and was probably a feature of West-Arabian altogether (cf. § 10 p).
4739.prule: No stress rule. Rabin infers that Himyaritic, like West-Arabian generally but more markedly, lacked an expiratory (stress) accent; the inference rests on al-Hamdānī's tenth-century characterisation of Himyaritic speech as 'halting' (muʿaqqad) and 'drawling' (yajurrūna fī kalāmihim), which Rabin equates with absence of stress accent. No stress position is stated or derivable.
4739.srule: Not mentioned in Rabin 1951 (ch. 5 §5 l-o, pp. 49-50, and ch. 10 §10 l-q, pp. 102-105, read in full): Rabin denies an expiratory (stress) accent for West-Arabian and Himyaritic altogether and never discusses secondary or rhythmic stress.
4739.quote: We get a more instructive indication in the term muʿaqqad 'halting' with which Hamdānī describes both Himyaritic itself and the dialects influenced by it. It seems that he means the same when he says that the people of Sarw Ḥimyar 'drawl' (yajurrūna fī kalāmihim). 'Drawling' in general is due to the absence of stress accent, and was probably a feature of West-Arabian altogether (cf. § 10 p). But South-Arabian must have had a drawling of a much more pronounced character, which produced the two-peak syllables of Minaean and other dialects (cf. Rhodokanakis, Studien, i, 12–56). It is this featur…
4739.loc: Ch. 5 'Himyar', §5 n, p. 49 (dli.ernet.103575); cross-references ch. 10 'Hijaz: the vowels', §10 m-p, pp. 102-105; the two p. 104 sentences quoted (§10 n and the opening sentence of §10 p, which sits at the foot of p. 104) are on p. 121
4739.idn: 'Himyaritic' (the language of Himyar) as described by al-Hamdani for tenth-century highland Yemen: pure 'halting' Himyaritic in the central mountain area around San'a' and the southern Sarat (Rabin ch. 5, pp. 42-45); data: No fieldwork: a philological study of medieval Arabic sources, chiefly al-Hamdani (d. 334/946)…
4739.exq_: It cannot be sufficiently stressed that these are merely impressionist terms: we are moving on ground that has not been satisfactorily investigated by modern phonetics. (pp. 102-103)
4739.tone: Rabin's frame (§10 m, p. 102) opposes an 'expiratory or stress accent' (English, German, Russian; in Semitic Hebrew, Aramaic; Syrian Arabic) to 'the opposite, non-expiratory type of accent' (French, American English, Indian languages, Amharic) in which 'slight expiratory prominence is lent to syllables by factors such as emphasis and sentence rhythm'; he places West-Arabian and, a fortiori, Himyaritic in the second type. He does not claim tone or a pitch accent for Himyaritic.
4739.sec_quote: It seems thus pretty well established that West-Arabian did not possess an expiratory stress.

4747.prule: Fixed final (rightmost) full stress, quantity-insensitive, stated as a reduction rule: every non-final syllable of a polysyllabic morpheme is stress-reduced (p.73), the first element of a compound or reduplicate is stress-reduced (p.72), and non-fully stressed syllables in a close-knit phrase precede the fully stressed one (p.70); only the final syllable is fully stressed and carries a canonical tone. Two degrees of reduction: first degree (vowel quality kept, length distinctions neutralised, sandhi tone o-s); second/extreme degree (final consonant lost, vowel -> [ə] = short /a/, all tonal distinctions lost = neutral tone/'architoneme'), the latter applying to Malay-loan syllables with SatM /ə/, which never occurs in final syllables (p.72). The /ə/ condition governs the DEGREE of reduction only, so placement is computable from syllable count. Every fully stressed syllable also bears one of five tentative tone phonemes (p.71, the tentative arrangement of the etic tones of Table III into phonemes) and stress is non-contrastive (Diller 1989 p.4). Court never writes 'stress falls on the final syllable'; the rule is the complement of the reduction statement, formulated over the polysyllabic morpheme, the compound/reduplicate and the close-knit phrase alike (domain word and phrase together), exactly as the catalog codes Central Thai (thai1261, Noss 1964: 'the last syllable in the phrase has at least normal stress', fixed-dominant final, domain 'word and phrase together', not strict).
4747.srule: None described: 'Non-final syllables in polysyllabic morphemes are subject to stress reduction' -- only the final syllable of a polysyllabic morpheme (and of a compound, reduplicate or close-knit phrase) is fully stressed; non-final syllables are reduced in two degrees set by the vowel (first degree: full vowel kept, sandhi tone; second degree: /ə/ syllables, neutral tone), not by position. The source characterises Miao as a whole as a syllable-tone language (every syllable carries a tone that distinguishes meaning; tone system of the same type as Chinese) and on p.105 places the Southwestern vernacular of the Huishui sub-dialect (c. 40,000 speakers; Yashui, Sandu, Doudi, Duanshan in Huishui County; Baitang, Zhongguo in Changshun County) inside that language. Translation of p.3: 'Miao has the general characteristics of Sino-Tibetan languages: 1. every syllable has a tone, and this tone distinguishes it in meaning from other syllables with the same initial and final; 2. the combination of sounds is rather restricted, e.g. only certain consonants may stand at the end of a syllable; 3. almost every syllable has lexical or grammatical meaning; polysyllabic simple words are few. Moreover, the tone system of Miao is entirely of the same kind as that of Chinese.'

4751.tone: Tonal: H, L, Rise, Fall plus an extra-high tone 'used sparingly... in only a few grammatical contexts' (Childs 1988: 22), chiefly the Negative Past/Perfective with final le (p. 73). The extra-high is measured as higher (155 vs 144 Hz), louder (82.9 vs 80.0 dB) and longer (199 vs 193 msec) than plain High (pp. 73-74, citing Childs 1988a = the 1989 paper 'The extra-high tone of Kisi: just another tone or a new system of prominence?', not obtained). Verbs are called 'accentual' in an autosegmental sense only: 'the Low tones on the verb being non-accented rather than associated with a tone' so that a floating High from a preceding name docks on the first verb syllable (p. 110). Footnote 4, p. 22: tone 'seems to be disappearing' within Atlantic, 'parallel to the changeover from tone to accent in many Benue-Congo languages' -- diachronic, not a Kisi stress statement. 4752.tone: Nelson 1952 p. 41-43: 'three registers of tone plus glides'; 'For this brief treatment of tone we shall mark them as follows: low, high, and mid, unmarked' (p. 42); tones 'not only lexical but also morphological'; glides on long vowels and 'quick glides on short vowels' (p. 43). Corroboration, second-hand: Czermak 1926 (Anthropos 21: 659, review of Lekens 1923 Spraakkunst der Ngbanditaal) reports tones tief/mittel/hoch plus glides tief-hoch, hoch-tief, tief-mittel, and: 'Um einem Worte mehr Nachdruck zu verleihen, wird eine Silbe, ohne die Intonierung zu verandern, exspiratorisch hervorgehoben, weshalb der Verfasser dem »Klemtoon« (dynamischem Akzent) ein eigenes Kapitel widmet' -- Lekens' 'klemtoon' is emphatic expiratory prominence that leaves tone unchanged, not a lexical or positional word stress; consistent with Nelson. Czermak says Lekens treats 'vorwiegend den Ostdialekt' (the eastern/northern variety).
